summary: This Standards Track document defines the HTTP QUERY method. It asks the target to process the enclosed content in a safe and idempotent manner and return the result. Like POST it can carry a body, but QUERY can be repeated or restarted without worrying about partial state changes.

eli5.summary: It is a way to ask a big, complicated question at a website without changing anything, and you can safely ask again.

questions: what is the http query method
http query vs get vs post
subtitle: A new HTTP method that carries a query in the request body while staying safe, idempotent and cacheable.

tldr.problem: Large queries do not fit well in a GET URI, and using POST for queries hides from clients and intermediaries that the request is safe and can be repeated.
tldr.mechanism: QUERY sends the query as request content, like POST, but is defined as safe and idempotent, like GET. Servers can also hand back URIs for the query or its result, and an Accept-Query header announces which query formats are supported.
tldr.outcome: Caching and automatic retries can work for queries with a body. RFC 10008 is a Proposed Standard, and IANA has registered the QUERY method and the Accept-Query field.

today: RFC 10008 is a Standards Track document with Proposed Standard status, published in June 2026. IANA has added the QUERY method and the Accept-Query field to its registries, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a QUERY Method
sections.content:
A common query pattern is GET /feed?q=foo&limit=10&sort=-published. It becomes a problem when the data is too voluminous for the URI. Size limits are often unknown because a request can pass through many uncoordinated systems (the HTTP specification recommends supporting at least 8000 octets). Encoding some data in a URI is inefficient, URIs are more likely to be logged and bookmarked than request content, and putting every combination of inputs in the URI casts each one as a distinct resource.

Many implementations use POST instead, but then it is not apparent, without specific knowledge of the server, that a safe and idempotent query is being performed. QUERY spans the gap: like POST, the input is the request content, but unlike POST the method is explicitly safe and idempotent, so caching and automatic retries can operate.

The RFC also follows the design principle that important resources ought to be identified by a URI, and describes how a server can assign URIs to the query itself or to a specific result.
sections.eli5: If your question is very long, writing it on the envelope does not work. QUERY puts it inside the envelope and tells everyone that just asking changes nothing.

sections.title: The QUERY Method
sections.content:
The content of the request and its media type define the query, and the origin server decides the scope of the operation from the target resource. The target URI's query part still helps identify the resource, but how it affects the result is specific to the resource and out of scope.

Servers MUST fail the request if the Content-Type is missing or inconsistent with the content.

QUERY requests are safe: the client does not request or expect any change to the target resource's state. The server may still create extra resources through which information can be retrieved. They are also idempotent, so they can be retried or repeated, for instance after a connection failure. A 200 (OK) response means the query was processed and the results are the response content.
sections.eli5: A QUERY is like asking a librarian to look something up. She does not rearrange the shelves, and you can ask again if she did not hear you.

sections.title: Media Types and Error Codes
sections.content:
The meaning of a QUERY depends on the request content and its metadata such as the media type, and any inconsistency MUST be rejected with a 4xx response. The RFC recommends specific codes:

  • No media type: fail with a 4xx such as 400.
  • Media type not supported by the resource: 415 (Unsupported Media Type). The Accept-Query field can tell the client what is supported.
  • Media type inconsistent with the actual content: 400 (Bad Request). A server is not allowed to infer a media type from the content and override a missing or wrong value, which is called content sniffing.
  • Type understood and content consistent, but the query cannot be processed: 422 (Unprocessable Content). An example is a syntactically correct SQL query that names a non-existent table.
  • Requested response type not supported through Accept: 406 (Not Acceptable).
sections.eli5: If the note is on the wrong kind of paper, or does not match what you said it was, the librarian says no and tells you why.

sections.title: Equivalent Resources, Location and Redirects
sections.content:
The equivalent resource of a QUERY is a resource that answers GET requests and represents that QUERY and its target, taking both the content and the metadata into account. Servers can but do not have to assign URIs to these.

A successful response can carry a Content-Location header that identifies a resource holding the results of the query just performed. A server can also put the URI of the equivalent resource in Location, which is a claim that a client can GET it to repeat the query without resending the content. Both URIs might be temporary, and if a later request fails the client can retry the original QUERY.

For redirects, 301, 302, 307 and 308 mean the client can send a similar QUERY to the new URI. The usual exception that turns a POST into a GET after 301 or 302 does not apply to QUERY. A 303 (See Other) says the query can be accomplished with a normal retrieval (a GET) of the URI in Location.
sections.eli5: After answering, the librarian may give you a ticket number. Next time you can show the ticket instead of copying the whole note again, but tickets can expire.

sections.title: Caching, Conditional and Range Requests
sections.content:
The response to a QUERY is cacheable. The cache key MUST incorporate the request content and related metadata. Caches MAY remove semantically insignificant differences first, such as content encodings, or normalize using format conventions (for example a +json suffix) or knowledge of the content's meaning. This only builds the key and does not change the request. Clients can use the no-transform cache directive to ask that no such transformation happens, though it is only advisory.

Caching QUERY is more complex than caching GET because the whole request content must be read to compute the key. If the response supplies a Location for an equivalent resource, clients can switch to GET and simplify processing.

For conditional requests, the selected representation is the same as for a GET to the equivalent resource, and the usual conditional header fields apply. Range requests behave like GET, but byte ranges offer little value for query results. Query formats usually have their own paging, such as FETCH FIRST ... ROWS ONLY in SQL, and those are expected to be used instead.
sections.eli5: A helper who remembers answers needs to remember the whole note, not just the desk number. If you got a ticket, using the ticket is quicker.

sections.title: The Accept-Query Header Field
sections.content:
A resource can use the Accept-Query response header to signal support for QUERY and to list the query format media types it accepts. The value is a list of media ranges in Structured Fields syntax, as Tokens or Strings without parameters. Media type parameters become Structured Field Parameters. Recipients MAY convert Tokens to Strings but MUST NOT process them differently by type. The order of the listed types is not significant.

The only supported wildcards are */* and xxxx/*. The value applies to every URI on the server that shares the same path, so the query component is ignored.

An example from the RFC is Accept-Query: "application/jsonpath", application/sql;charset="UTF-8". Clients can also discover QUERY support with an OPTIONS request and the Allow field, or just try a QUERY and look for a 4xx such as 405 or 415.
sections.eli5: A sign on the library door lists which kinds of notes the librarian can read, such as SQL or JSONPath.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
QUERY is subject to the general security considerations of all HTTP methods. Putting request information in the content rather than the URI is preferred in some cases, since URIs are more likely to be logged by intermediaries. When the query holds sensitive information, the potential logging of the URI can be a reason to choose QUERY over GET.

If a server creates a temporary resource for the results and assigns it a URI (for Location or Content-Location), and the request has sensitive information that cannot be logged, the URI SHOULD NOT include sensitive portions of the original content.

Caches that normalize QUERY content incorrectly, or differently from how the resource processes it, can return a wrong response after a false-positive match. A QUERY from a user agent implementing CORS needs a preflight request, because QUERY is not one of the CORS-safelisted methods.
sections.eli5: Do not write secrets on the ticket number, because tickets can be seen by lots of people along the way.
